name: Baring Brothers

summary.text: Baring Brothers & Co. was a London merchant bank. In 1888 a Barings-led flotation of the Buenos Aires Water Supply and Drainage Company failed to sell, and by November 1890 the firm, heavily exposed to Argentina under senior partner Edward Baring (Lord Revelstoke), could not meet its obligations and told the Bank of England. An accountant's report found it solvent but illiquid. The Bank of England organised a guarantee fund of about £17 million from City institutions; the old firm's assets were liquidated under the Bank's management and a new Baring Brothers & Co. Ltd took over the trade-finance business. The guarantee was extended in 1893 and Barings was released from it in 1895.

sources.publisher: Bank Underground (Bank of England staff blog)
sources.title: Rescuing a SIFI, Halting a Panic: the Barings Crisis of 1890

facts.claim: A Barings-led flotation of the Buenos Aires Water Supply and Drainage Company failed in 1888, leaving the firm over-exposed to Argentina.
facts.quote: A Barings-led flotation of the Buenos Aires Water Supply and Drainage Company flopped in 1888

sources.publisher: Bank Underground (Bank of England staff blog)
sources.title: Rescuing a SIFI, Halting a Panic: the Barings Crisis of 1890
How to Prevent a Banking Panic: the Barings Crisis of 1890

facts.claim: The Baring Archive attributes the 1890 crisis to poor decision-making by the then senior partner, Edward 'Ned' Baring, Lord Revelstoke.
facts.quote: poor decision making by the then senior partner, Ned Revelstoke

sources.title: 250th Anniversary Symposium: Barings History and Archives

facts.claim: In November 1890 rumours circulated that Barings might have no surplus after paying its liabilities; the accountant's report ordered by Governor Lidderdale found the firm solvent but illiquid.
facts.quote: That report showed a solvent but illiquid Barings.

sources.publisher: Bank Underground (Bank of England staff blog)
sources.title: Rescuing a SIFI, Halting a Panic: the Barings Crisis of 1890

facts.claim: Britannica states that the Bank of England, with the leading joint-stock banks, took over Barings' liabilities amounting to £21,000,000.
facts.quote: the Bank, in conjunction with the leading joint-stock banks of the United Kingdom, took over Baring's liabilities amounting to £21,000,000.

facts.claim: The 1890 rescue was structured as a guarantee fund of about £17.1 million in which a syndicate of banks would rateably share any loss from Barings' liquidation over four years; the firm was reconstructed as a limited company, Baring Brothers & Co. Ltd.
facts.quote: The guarantee fund of £17.1 million included all institutions, and some of the largest shares were assigned to banks whose inattentive lending had permitted Barings to swell its portfolio.

sources.publisher: Bank Underground (Bank of England staff blog)
sources.title: Rescuing a SIFI, Halting a Panic: the Barings Crisis of 1890

facts.claim: The Bank of England describes the 1890 operation as a 'lifeboat' rescue of a firm perceived to be solvent; the guarantee period was extended by one year in 1893 and Barings was released from its guarantee to the Bank in 1895.
facts.quote: 'lifeboat' approach to rescue Barings which was perceived to be solvent

sources.title: The Bank of England's Balance Sheet: Monetary Policy and Liquidity Provision during the Financial Crisis

connections.claim: Barings notified the Bank of England of its difficulties in early November 1890; the Bank organised the guarantee fund and managed the liquidation of the old firm's assets.
connections.quote: a "bad bank" that retained its name and its toxic assets, managed by the Bank of England

sources.publisher: Bank Underground (Bank of England staff blog)
sources.title: Rescuing a SIFI, Halting a Panic: the Barings Crisis of 1890
How to Prevent a Banking Panic: the Barings Crisis of 1890

connections.claim: Governor William Lidderdale ordered the accountant's report on Barings in November 1890, refused the Chancellor's letter, and later negotiated a one-year extension of the guarantee in 1893.
connections.quote: Lidderdale ordered an accountant's report on Barings.

sources.publisher: Bank Underground (Bank of England staff blog)

openQuestions: The site's 'real GDP fell about 11% in 1890–91' for Argentina and the role of President Juárez Celman were not covered by the sources consulted.

The site says the Bank of England 'judged that its failure could bring down the London acceptance market'; the sources describe the rescue as halting a panic but this precise judgement was not quoted.
One secondary source (Sagix) gives a £7.5 million guarantee fund; Bank Underground gives £17.1 million for the fund and £7.5 million for a Bank advance.
